newsitem.title: USA: U.S. to open trade missions to more public scrutiny.
newsitem.headline: U.S. to open trade missions to more public scrutiny.

text.p: Commerce Secretary William Daley on Monday unveiled a plan to open the agency's trade missions to more public scrutiny in response to accusations they had been used to raise political money.
"Trade missions are an essential element of a broad-based policy designed to increase job opportunities for all Americans," Daley said at a news conference.

"They are not private rewards for the individuals and companies that participate in them," he added. "However, these missions can succeed only if the American people are confident that they in fact serve the public interest."

Daley said the new policy, which went into effect on Monday after a 30-day review during which the commercial trips had been suspended, puts partisan political considerations off limits in selecting corporate participants.

The missions usually involve Commerce Department officials accompanied by corporate executives and are touted as a way to develop business and new export opportunities for American companies. Sometimes missions are led by the secretary.

Judicial Watch, a conservative legal group, has sued the Department of Commerce for documents relating to trade missions. The group accused the late Commerce Secretary Ron Brown of using the commercial missions to raise money for President Bill Clinton and the Democratic Party.
The department has denied those allegations.

The group has also turned its attention to former Commerce Department official John Huang, whose fund-raising activities for the Democratic National Committee have come under fire amid growing questions about the legality of some of the contributions. The group questioned Huang just before last November's presidential election as part of the court proceeding.
Daley said the 30-day review did not include scrutiny of past trade missions.

"In our review of the last 30 days, we looked at the procedures and criteria that have been in place and looked at them from a perspective of how do we strengthen them to make sure these missions accomplish what they want, that they assure the American people that they are done in a way that they would be proud of and that there is no issue as to the integrity that goes into them," Daley said.
He said the review also evaluated the value of high-level Commerce Department officials taking corporate executives on overseas trips to try to drum up business for U.S. companies.

"We cannot -- and will not -- unilaterally withdraw in a world in which our economic competitors are using all the tools at their disposal to pursue market opportunities aggressively for their companies," Daley said.

The new policy sets a procedure for developing missions and an open process for selecting corporate participants. Proposed missions will be subject to review and approval by a department panel, which Daley said would be comprised of mostly career officials.
